div.p: We suggest and compare different methods for estimating spatial autoregressive models with randomly missing data in the dependent variable. Aside from the traditional expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, a nonlinear least squares method is suggested and a generalized method of moments estimation is developed for the model. A two-stage least squares estimation with imputation is proposed as well. We analytically compare these estimation methods and find that generalized nonlinear least squares, best generalized twostage least squares with imputation and best method of moments estimators have identical asymptotic variances. These methods are less efficient than maximum likelihood estimation implemented with the EM algorithm. When unknown heteroscedasticity exists, however, EM estimation produces inconsistent estimates. Under this situation, these methods outperform EM. We provide finite sample evidence through Monte Carlo experiments.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Spatial models have extensively been used in regional science and geography, (see, e.g. Cliff andOrd, 1981, andAnselin, 1988), and many economic processes that concern spatial dependence among cross-sectional units have prompted increasing attention to these models. Examples of such processes include housing decision, technology adoption, tax competition, welfare participation and price decision. Given this heightened interest, spatial econometric models are currently being applied in urban, environmental, labour, and developmental economics, among others. The most popular is the spatial autoregressive (SAR) model, for which many estimation methods have recently been developed and studied. Kelejian and Prucha (1998) suggest a twostage least squares (2SLS) estimator, which is computationally simple but inefficient relative to a maximum likelihood (ML) estimator. Lee (2004) proves the consistency and asymptotic normality of the quasi-maximum likelihood estimators of the SAR model. Lee (2007) proposes a generalized method of moments (GMMs) procedure based on linear and quadratic moment functions, and shows that a best GMM estimator may have the same limiting distribution as an ML estimator. Kelejian and Prucha (2010a) and Lin and Lee (2010) study related GMM estimation methods for the SAR model with heteroscedastic disturbances. However, these estimation methods are designed primarily for models with fully observed data.

In practice, missing data are a common problem that researchers face. Numerous methods designed to address this problem can be found in literature on statistics and econometrics. Some of these approaches include listwise deletion, pairwise deletion, expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, and multiple imputation (see, e.g. Allison, 2001). When it comes up to spatial models, however, some simple methods, such as listwise deletion, are unsuitable because of interdependence among the components of the dependent variable vector. Simple deletion of unobserved data from samples may yield inconsistent estimates. The SAR model is a general equilibrium model, in which the number of units can be regarded as a population. Thus, omission of relevant units creates an approximated model with misspecification in the weights matrix of an SAR model, thereby resulting in failure to capture the full structure of the population. In using the SAR model to study network effects on outcomes (Lee et al., 2010), the deletion of units due to missing observations results in the omission of some nodes and deletion of links in a network. Kelejian and Prucha (2010b) consider various configurations of the missing observations in spatial models with spatially lagged dependent variables. They find that in one case, the missing observations are asymptotically negligible; while in another case, they are not. In empirical literature, an imputation method is commonly used as an alternative to the simple deletion method, in which some 'fitted values' are first used in the place of missing data, and then traditional methods are used for estimation. Aside from imputation methods, other estimation procedures can be applied to certain situations, such as when data are missing only from the dependent variable. One of these approaches is a likelihood-based approach, such as the EM algorithm. LeSage and Pace (2004) apply the EM algorithm to the SAR model and linear regression models with spatially correlated disturbances.

In this paper, we consider a case in which observations are missing only from the dependent variable. In regional studies, exogenous variables may be available from different sources rather than from data available on a local government web site. Examples include censuses that provide regional demographic data, which can be aggregated to regional-level data. Thus, studying the case in which missing data are only in the dependent variable can be practically useful. SAR models with either homoscedastic or heteroscedastic disturbances are considered. We suggest three simple and robust estimation procedures for the model. The first one is a GMM estimation based on linear moments; the second one is nonlinear least squares (NLS) estimation, in which the reduced form of the SAR model is used; and the third one is a 2SLS estimation with imputation (I2SLS). We analytically compare the asymptotic properties of these estimation methods and investigate their finite sample performance.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides the model specification and three suggested estimation procedures. We begin with a basic SAR model with i.i.d. disturbances and illustrate how our estimation system handles missing data in the dependent variable. We prove the consistency and asymptotic normality of our proposed estimators. Best choices in linear moments for GMM (BGMM) estimation, generalized NLS (GNLS) estimation, and best generalized I2SLS (IBG2SLS) are presented, and a comparison of the asymptotic relative efficiency of the estimators is made. In Section 3, we consider models with heteroscedastic disturbances and compare our estimation methods with likelihood-based approaches, such as ML estimation with the EM algorithm. Section 4 discusses the Monte Carlo experiments that we conduct, and Section 5 concludes the paper. All the proofs are provided in the appendices.

div.head: THE SAR MODEL WITH HETEROSCEDASTIC DISTURBANCES
div.p: In this section, we investigate the robustness of the proposed estimation methods against unknown heteroscedasticity. div.head: MONTE CARLO RESULTS
div.p: To investigate the finite sample performance of the estimation methods, we conduct Monte Carlo experiments, designed as follows. The SAR model has two regressors x i,1 and x i,2 . The (x i,1 , x i,2 )'s are independent of all i. The true parameters are λ 0 = 0.3, β 10 = 1 and β 20 = 1.

We first consider the model with i.i.d. disturbances, where the i 's are independently drawn from N(0, 1) and are independent of x i,1 and x i,2 . x i,1 and x i,2 are generated from N(0, 1). After this, we consider one of the regressor as a constant intercept term, as well as a non-normal distribution for i .

For weights matrix W n , we follow the design of Arraiz et al. (2010), which is referred to as the 'circular world matrix'. We also conduct experiments on another design for the weights matrix. We adopt this matrix design for two reasons. First, want to avoid designing an excessively dense matrix, i.e. one with too many non-zero elements. Because dense weights matrices sometimes cause poor performance of the estimators, using them may generate less interesting experiment results. Second, given that we investigate the performance of all the methods under heteroscedastic disturbances, we follow the heteroscedasticity design proposed by Arraiz et al. (2010). The weights matrix is designed as follows. For the n × n weights matrix, the first n/3 rows (except for the first row) have zeroes everywhere, except for the elements in positions (i, i + 1) and (i, i -1). In the first row, the non-zero elements are in positions (1, 2) and (1, n) so that it relates to a circular world. The non-zero elements in the first n/3 rows are all random draws from U (0, 1); i.e. we allow the neighbours to asymmetrically affect one another. 13 Then, these rows are row normalized so that the sum of each row is equal to 1. The next n/3 rows (say, j = n/3 + 1, . . . , 2n/3) have zeroes everywhere, except in positions (j, j ± r), where r = 1, 2, . . . , 5. The non-zero elements are designed in the same fashion as those in the first n/3 rows. The last n/3 rows are defined in a similar manner to the first n/3 rows. Specifically, the non-zero elements in rows j = 2n/3 + 1, . . . , n -1 are in positions (j, j + 1) and (j, j -1); in the last row, the non-zero elements are in positions (n, 1) and (n, n -1). The non-zero elements in these rows are also designed in the same fashion as those in the first 2n/3 rows. The weights matrix is a sparse weights matrix, with each individual having only several 'neighbours'. The number of neighbours differs for each individual, depending on its position. When we design heteroscedastic disturbances, we use this 'number of neighbours' as a determinant of variances.

For sample sizes, we set n from 'small', n = 60 and 'moderate', n = 180, to 'large', n = 540. 14 For missing observations, the y i 's of the first α% of the n individuals are unobserved for each sample size n, where α is set as 10, 25 and 50.

We compare the estimation results of BGMM, GNLS and IBG2SLS estimations, as well as those of the EM algorithm proposed by LeSage and Pace (2004). 15 Initial consistent estimates used in all three estimations are the NLSE without weighting. For EM estimation, we follow LeSage and Pace (2004).

For comparison, we also report the results of an ML estimation by excluding all the observations with missing data. This approach is the simple 'data deletion' method. After deletion, we have fewer observations; therefore, we reformulate a smaller weights matrix for the remaining observations using the corresponding elements in the n × n weights matrix. We then perform row normalization. We also determine whether the estimation results derived using the simple data deletion method in the spatial context will generate serious biases.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: We consider an SAR model with randomly missing data in the dependent variable. To estimate the model, we propose GMM estimation, NLS estimation and 2SLS estimation with imputation. In GMM estimation, the reduced form of the model is used to derive the expectation of each missing data as a function of the observed independent variables and parameters to be estimated. The expectation is then used to replace the missing data. After the substitution, the transformed disturbances retain zero mean, which yields orthogonality of instruments and disturbances as linear moment conditions for GMM estimation. We prove that the GMM estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal. Within the estimation framework, we derive the best of choice of IVs. In NLS estimation, the reduced form of the model is used and also generates consistent estimates. In 2SLS estimation with imputation, the simpler NLS estimator is used to construct filled values of missing data, and then 2SLS estimation with imputation is performed. We compare the three methods and find that BGMME, GNLSE and IBG2SLSE are asymptotically equivalent.

We also study the case for the SAR model with unknown heteroscedastic disturbances. Given that our estimation methods use linear moment condition for estimation, which only requires zero-mean disturbances, the estimates are consistent under unknown heteroscedasticity. By contrast, the conventional EM algorithm does not yield consistent estimates. Therefore, our estimation methods serve as good alternatives under unknown heteroscedasticity.

We design Monte Carlo experiments to study the finite sample properties of the estimation methods. The results show that under homoscedastic disturbances, the EM algorithm yields relatively efficient estimates. However, BGMM, GNLS and BG2SLS with imputation outperform the EM approach when unknown heteroscedasticity exists.

Because BGMM, GNLS and IBG2SLS are asymptotically equivalent and have similar finite sample properties, any one of these approaches can be used in estimation under practical situations. In terms of testing issues (not discussed in this study), however, the BGMM approach provides a flexible framework. Given that the BGMM approach is also an OGMM approach, it provides a valid framework for statistical inference via over-identification test, distance test and gradient test in addition to the Wald test (Newey and West, 1987).

We can extend our estimation frameworks from an SAR(1) model to an SAR(p) model. Lee and Liu (2010) extend GMM estimation frameworks from SAR(1) to SAR(p) models for complete observations. For missing observations, this extension should be straightforward because the linear moment conditions used in the current paper are valid not only for an SAR(1), but also for an SAR(p) model.

div.head: APPENDIX E: COMPUTATION OF S -1 n (λ)
div.p: From a computational point of view, a concern is the evaluation of the inverse of S n (λ) = I n -λW n because many estimators involve S -1 n (λ). This problem is a particularly genuine concern for large sample sizes given that W n is a large dimensional matrix. Lee (2003) discusses the computation of S -1 n (λ)b n , where b n is an n × 1 vector. Such methods can also be used in the current work to evaluate S -1 n (λ). We present a contraction mapping algorithm.

Because λW n < 1 for some matrix norm • is usually assumed, we have S -1 n (λ) = ∞ i=0 λ i W i n (Kelejian andPrucha, 1998, andLee, 2003). In this case, a finite expansion m i=0 λ i W i n for some sufficiently large m can be used to approximate S -1 n (λ). In practice, an appropriate number of terms m should be selected to derive a reasonably accurate approximation. This selection can be efficiently achieved with a contraction mapping algorithm, described as follows. Consider mapping T (Q) = I n + λW n Q, where Q is a squared matrix. Because λW n < 1, T is a contracting mapping given that T (Q 1 ) -T (Q 2 ) ≤ γ Q 1 -Q 2 with γ = λW n for all Q 1 and Q 2 . Starting with any initial squared matrix Q 1 , we define the iteration as
div.formula: Q i+1 = T (Q i ) = I n + λW n Q i . Thus, T (Q i ) -T (Q i+1 ) ≤ γ Q i -Q i+1 = γ T (Q i-1 ) -T (Q i ) ≤ • • • ≤ γ i Q 1 -Q 2 = γ i (I n -λW n )Q 1 -I n .
div.p: If Q 1 is taken to be I n , for example, then T (Q i ) -T (Q i+1 ) ≤ γ i+1 . The iteration can stop with a given error criteria ε (a small positive scalar, say 10 -6 ). Any value Q i * +1 such that T (Q i * ) -T (Q i * +1 ) < ε can be taken as solution Q for Q = I n + λW n Q, i.e. Q i * +1 is the desired approximation of S -1 n (λ). The rate of convergence of this fixed-point algorithm is geometric. The number of iterations required to achieve the error criteria within ε can be predicted.
